entities.name: Mahmud al-Kashgari
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mahmud al-Kashgari (died 1101 CE) was a pivotal 11th-century Kara-Khanid Turkic scholar, linguist, and cartographer whose monumental work, *Diwan Lughat al-Turk* (Compendium of the Turkic Dialects), preserved and systematized the Turkic languages at a critical juncture of their expansion and interaction with the Arabo-Persianate world. Operating from the cultural crossroads of Kashgar in Central Asia, his efforts provided an indispensable linguistic and ethnographic record of the Turkic peoples, offering a window into their culture, history, and geographical distribution during the medieval period. His work served as a crucial bridge between the emerging Turkic literary traditions and the established Islamic scholarly milieu, significantly influencing subsequent Turkic lexicography and cultural self-awareness.

The *Diwan Lughat al-Turk*, completed between 1072 and 1074 CE and presented to the Abbasid Caliph al-Muqtadi in Baghdad, is a comprehensive dictionary of Turkic languages, primarily Chagatai and other Oğuz dialects, meticulously written in Arabic. It contains over 7,500 words, including proverbs, poems, riddles, and folk tales, all translated into Arabic, thereby providing a vast corpus of early Turkic oral literature. Beyond its linguistic utility, the *Diwan* also includes a unique circular world map, the *Diwan Lughat al-Turk Map*, which depicts the known world with Turkic lands at its center, showcasing Kashgari's geographical knowledge and ethnocentric perspective. This encyclopedic approach captured the linguistic diversity and cultural richness of Turkic tribes from the borders of China to Eastern Europe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mahmud al-Kashgari's *Diwan Lughat al-Turk* is a foundational work for Turkic linguistics and ethnography, preserving invaluable data that shaped the understanding of Turkic identity and history. It influenced subsequent Turkic scholarship and contributed significantly to cultural self-awareness across Central Asia and the Near East.
